rationale: A wins because it keeps its hands on the evidence and makes the proof gaps useful instead of decorative. Its line, "the competitor take rates a reporter will compare against must be supplied, not guessed," is exactly the discipline this assignment needed. B has smart bones, but "Substack is building a TikTok-style feed without the ad model" asserts a business-model fact the update did not give it. That is how a decent angle gets itself killed in the first reporter follow-up.
gaps_in_A: "One writer's case for moving video and podcasts onto Substack under a 10% cut" is a real angle only if Substack can produce the writer. The set says that, but it should flag the angle as conditional, not ready.
"Substack creators earned $400M last year" as a standalone story is killed too broadly. A sharper data angle around what "top creators" means and what Substack will not disclose could work.
"Next step: meanest-editor" is process noise. The founder needs fact-checking and source-gathering before drafting, not another internal skill label.
gaps_in_B: "Substack is building a TikTok-style feed without the ad model" is unsupported. The update says TikTok-style feed and 10% subscription cut; it does not say no ads.
"Substack's feed is funded by a 10% cut of paid subscriptions" turns a take-rate fact into a funding claim. That needs confirmation before it becomes a headline.
"its revenue is capped at 10% of subscriptions" overstates the facts. The update gives one revenue cut, not Substack's entire revenue model.

"whether subscription economics can sustain an attention product" and "a 10% cut can pay for a full media platform" are too close. One is the cleaner business-model angle; the other is wearing the same suit with a different tie.
